The Riga settlement also remained part of the legal relationship between Warsaw and Moscow. Polish diplomacy referred to it in the nonaggression pact concluded with the Soviet Union in 1932. The dispute in 1939 therefore concerned a state with existing treaty relations, rather than an unallocated borderland. Its eastern provinces contained Polish, Ukrainian, Belarusian, and Jewish communities, among others. Their diverse attachments could not be reduced to the territorial preferences of Berlin or Moscow. Recognition of that diversity requires attention to the inhabitants; it does not confer a right upon foreign governments to dispose of them.

properties.note: Read Reading the offensive; Measuring the advance. The Polish commands were arranged around the territory they had to defend. Army Pomorze under Władysław Bortnowski covered the Corridor; Army Modlin under Emil Krukowicz-Przedrzymirski faced the threat from East Prussia. Farther west and south stood Tadeusz Kutrzeba’s Army Poznań, Juliusz Rómmel’s Army Łódź and Antoni Szylling’s Army Kraków. Army Karpaty covered the southeastern approaches, the Narew Operational Group the northeast, and Army Prusy formed the principal strategic reserve. Their names are useful geographical guides, but the spaces between these forces were as consequential as their individual positions. Germany’s converging advances threatened to separate them, close their withdrawal routes and commit the reserves before those reserves were fully assembled.

properties.note: Read The order and the pretext; Crossings and strongpoints. By the time German troops crossed the frontier, Germany had been preparing its attack for months. The army’s plan, Fall Weiss , aimed to destroy Poland’s armed forces before they could escape the converging German offensives. The destruction of Czechoslovakia earlier in the year had enlarged Germany’s southern approaches into Poland, giving military planners another direction from which to threaten the Polish rear. Their task was to exploit that geography quickly enough to prevent an effective defence from taking shape.

Filipowicz’s brigade disengaged in organized fashion, although some elements moved independently after dark. Juliusz S. Holding a position, passing a message and preserving a formation for the next day were all parts of the same defence.

The Soviet Politburo’s resolution of October 2 directed the release of specified private soldiers from the Soviet-occupied eastern territories, retained others for road construction, and concentrated private soldiers from German-occupied districts pending negotiations with Germany. A man’s home district and status could determine which power detained him, or whether he was retained for forced labour.

The frontier deployment concentrated both sides around a few operational problems. North of the Pripet Marshes, the German armies could converge on the Soviet forces projecting west around Białystok, then threaten the crossings leading into the interior. Hitler’s written decision of 21 August 1941 put Ukraine ahead of an immediate assault on Moscow. Destroying Soviet forces in the south, securing the Donets industrial region, taking the Crimea and interrupting oil supplies from the Caucasus received priority. Leningrad and contact with Finland remained objectives in the north. The decision was consequential, but it was not a choice between an available victory and an inexplicable diversion. The alternative submitted three days earlier also required repair, concentration and the successful conclusion of battles still in progress.

properties.note: Read A city connected by water; Fighting for the approaches; Isolation and the attempt to reverse it. On 8 September 1941, German troops reached Shlisselburg at the point where the Neva leaves Lake Ladoga. Leningrad’s remaining overland connection with the Soviet interior was cut. The city itself remained in Soviet hands, and routes across the lake remained available. The immediate question was whether those routes could carry enough food, fuel and ammunition to sustain a great city and its defenders. A waterway on which movement was possible was not yet a supply service adequate to the task. Ships, landing places, labour and distribution now set limits on how long soldiers and households could endure.

properties.note: Read Fighting for the approaches. The 291st Rifle Division illustrates this competition. Its battalions had been intended for the northern bank of the Neva, but the situation around Beloostrov and Sestroretsk drew them towards the Karelian Isthmus instead. Finnish advances there influenced where Soviet troops could be used. The Leningrad Front report of 3 September, issued at 22.00, also described the depleted formations already defending the isthmus. In the 198th Rifle Division, it recorded only six heavy machine guns; that division’s 450th Rifle Regiment had three hundred men and no machine guns. The regiment’s figure must not be mistaken for the strength of the entire division, nor attributed to the incoming 291st. Commanders were moving formations whose nominal titles concealed very different capacities. A division arriving from elsewhere might hold a sector that a division exhausted by retreat could no longer defend. The report establishes the equipment shortage at that moment; it cannot by itself reconstruct every loss that produced it.

The southern movement developed from the German bridgehead near Kremenchuk. A bridgehead is more than a foothold on the opposite bank: to support a major advance it must provide space for troops to assemble, crossings through which heavy equipment can pass and routes that allow columns to disperse after crossing. In his retrospective account, Guderian credited Colonel Albert Praun with establishing a telephone connection from Romny to Kleist’s group through Lokhvytsia and Lubny. German mobile formations had moved through the breaches left by Vyazma and Bryansk, but the pocket battles still consumed troops and the Soviet command had placed new forces along approach sectors. properties.note: Read What the evacuation order required. Resolution 801 named institutions, destinations and responsible officials. Molotov was to notify foreign missions that they should evacuate to Kuibyshev. The Presidium of the Supreme Soviet and the government were to go east, with Molotov among those assigned to move. The organs of the defence and navy commissariats were ordered out, and the principal group of the General Staff was to move to Arzamas. Kaganovich was charged with providing trains, while Beria's security apparatus was to arrange protection. These clauses show that “evacuate the government” was not a single train leaving a station. It was a coordinated relocation of diplomatic, administrative, military and security functions, each dependent on rail capacity and on decisions about what must remain in the capital.

The U.S. Army narrative describes looting and signs of disintegration after the loss of Kalinin and the danger to the capital became clear. Steinhardt later reported unrest before the transfer and deterioration after it became public. These sources support a crisis; they do not justify saying that every resident fled or that the entire municipal administration ceased to function. A city of millions held people making different decisions under different constraints. Some sought a train out, some carried on working, some joined defence labour or militia, and some had nowhere to go. A narrative of total collapse would make those differences disappear.

properties.note: Read Outer front and inner defence. Unrest was not confined to Moscow. On 19 October, workers in Ivanovo attacked administrative and Party premises and officials, according to Mark Edele's account. Some raised the demand for soviets without Communists: a challenge to Party authority expressed through the language of Soviet institutions. This was a civilian disturbance, not an army mutiny, and it belongs to Ivanovo rather than to a count of incidents in the capital. It nevertheless reveals a tension in wartime mobilisation. A state requiring continued labour and sacrifice could encounter opposition from the very workers in whose name it claimed to govern. The Moscow decree attempted to contain disorder locally within that wider political crisis.

Georgy Zhukov commanded the Western Front forces defending the outer approaches. Lieutenant General Pavel Artemev, identified in the translation as chief of the Moscow garrison, held responsibility for the near approaches. Major General Kuzma Sinilov, the Moscow commandant, was charged with order in the city. These were overlapping layers of defence and governance, not three rival commanders each directing the entire battle. Their separation reflects a practical fact: the person assigning divisions on the Mozhaisk road could not also direct every curfew pass, urban patrol and antiaircraft movement. The government attempted to make the chain of command legible before an emergency could collapse it.

properties.note: Read Outer front and inner defence; Residents inside the new regime; The fight outside the decree. Zhukov's command had already changed as the threat widened. He had taken over the combined Western and Reserve Fronts on 10 October; on the seventeenth, the Stavka created Kalinin Front under Ivan Konev to handle the northern flank. properties.note: Read What “siege” meant on this date. The capital's emergency joined political survival to military defence, but the wider war continued to threaten the resources on which both rested. In eastern Ukraine, German forces were approaching Kharkov, another major industrial and railway centre. The Soviet state was trying to preserve institutions in Moscow and productive capacity elsewhere under the pressure of simultaneous advances. The next test was whether its armies, transport and industrial evacuation could continue functioning as important cities farther south passed into enemy hands.

properties.note: Read Kharkov on the twenty-fourth; Industry as a moving target. Kharkov, now Kharkiv, contained a substantial Jewish community as well as its factories and railways. The Encyclopaedia Judaica account records that many Jews left before German occupation. It does not establish a common reason why others remained, and their circumstances should not be replaced by assumptions about ignorance, confidence or choice. Those still in the city now faced authorities whose persecution of Jews was already established elsewhere. The mass killings associated with Kharkov's later occupation had not all occurred on 24 October. The immediate change was that escape and ordinary life would now be governed by the power of the occupiers.

On 24 October 1941, German Sixth Army took Kharkov, the industrial and railway city in eastern Ukraine. The event occurred while Moscow remained under an emergency regime and Army Group Centre struggled along its own approach roads. Neither development was a subordinate footnote to the other. On 24 October 1941, German Sixth Army took Kharkov, the industrial and railway city in eastern Ukraine. The event occurred while Moscow remained under an emergency regime and Army Group Centre struggled along its own approach roads. Neither development was a subordinate footnote to the other. Army Group South, commanded by Gerd von Rundstedt, pursued a cluster of objectives: Kharkov, the Donets industrial basin, the route towards Rostov and the entrance to the Crimea. Its armies did not move at the same speed or along a single axis. The capture of Kharkov was a clear change of control on this date, but it did not mean that the entire Soviet southern front collapsed or that Germany had gained the city's evacuated machinery.

There was a second difference between a reserve on paper and one available to Zhukov. A unit transferred from another front could strengthen Moscow while weakening the sector it left. A newly formed unit could preserve that other front but arrive less prepared. Neither choice was inherently irrational. The Stavka had to weigh the risk of a sudden German thrust through the capital's approaches against continuing threats at Leningrad and in the south. Officers examining rail schedules, commanders defending the line and civilians queuing for transport encountered different parts of the same allocation problem. The apparent stillness of the front gave the Soviet leadership a chance to make choices, but not the certainty that those choices would be sufficient.

On 9 November, German troops held the railway junction at Tikhvin, captured the previous day. The loss threatened the supply of Leningrad far beyond the battlefield. Since September, food and ammunition had crossed Lake Ladoga to reach the besieged city, but the lake route depended on cargo first arriving at its eastern approaches. properties.note: Read How the thrust developed; What the attack cost both armies. The German offensive towards Tikhvin opened on 16 October, as dated by Kirchubel and the Russian official account of the subsequent operation. It drove through the boundary between Soviet Fourth and Fifty-Second Armies, east of the Volkhov. Soviet commanders were themselves preparing attacks to restore communications with Leningrad, so the German movement disrupted an active effort rather than simply crossing an undefended region. The advance then slowed in difficult ground and worsening conditions. Reaching Tikhvin required several weeks of fighting and renewed movement; the town's eventual capture should not conceal the resistance and material strain accumulated along the way.

properties.note: Read The Ladoga supply chain. Ladoga transport had begun well before the Tikhvin crisis. The Presidential Library's chronology records the first food convoy reaching Osinovets on the western shore on 12 September, with grain and, separately, ammunition arriving that day. This early movement established a working route after the land blockade began. It did not remove dependence on transport approaching the lake from the Soviet interior. Tikhvin's capture struck that upstream connection. The emergency was therefore a deterioration of an existing supply system, not the sudden invention of lake transport after the railway was lost. The vessels and landing places could remain available while the means of bringing cargo to them became less capable.

The northern objective was to tighten the pressure on Leningrad and seek a connection with Finnish forces farther north. The Soviet command could not respond by concentrating all available resources around the capital. It had to sustain the northern front and preserve a route to a city whose survival depended on outside supply. Tikhvin thus mattered to the wider campaign without being a subsidiary episode of Typhoon. It was a separate operation with a direct relationship to the siege, fought by forces whose next decisions would affect people far from the town itself.

Six weeks earlier, Typhoon had begun with the prospect of destroying the armies defending Moscow before a prolonged campaign became necessary. The Vyazma and Bryansk encirclements inflicted the expected catastrophe, but the expected end of resistance did not follow. Soviet forces rebuilt the approaches, government institutions survived the evacuation crisis and Tula remained defended. The question facing Germany had consequently changed. It was no longer whether a major Soviet defeat could be achieved; October had answered that. It was whether the depleted attacking force could now secure a strategic result that its earlier victory had failed to deliver.

properties.note: Read The day before another attempt; Three army groups, three problems; What Orsha revealed; Roads, weather and repair; Civilians and occupation. On 13 November, German chiefs of staff met at Orsha to discuss how much more their armies could accomplish. The figures before them described a force seriously diminished by five months of war. The next day, Army Group Centre was still preparing another attempt against Moscow, while Soviet Forty-Ninth Army attacked near Serpukhov. The phase closes at this conjunction: German leaders had acknowledged the limits of their means but continued to demand an offensive, and Soviet commanders were doing more than waiting for it. The renewed German attacks would begin on the northern wing on 15 November, with the major mobile thrusts following on subsequent days.

Army Group North still held Tikhvin, taken on 8 November, but possession of the rail junction had not delivered Leeb's full objective. Soviet forces were contesting the German salient, and the hoped-for link with Finnish forces near the Svir had not been made. The railway towards Ladoga remained cut while the town was German-held, so Leningrad's supply crisis persisted. But Leeb needed troops both to defend the salient and to maintain the broader siege line. The U.S. Army history reports that by this stage he had exhausted his reserves reaching Tikhvin. A commander can win a local objective and still be unable to turn it into the next strategic step.

Army Group North still held Tikhvin, taken on 8 November, but possession of the rail junction had not delivered Leeb's full objective. Soviet forces were contesting the German salient, and the hoped-for link with Finnish forces near the Svir had not been made. The railway towards Ladoga remained cut while the town was German-held, so Leningrad's supply crisis persisted. But Leeb needed troops both to defend the salient and to maintain the broader siege line. The U.S. Army history reports that by this stage he had exhausted his reserves reaching Tikhvin. A commander can win a local objective and still be unable to turn it into the next strategic step.

properties.note: Read What the staff already knew. The shortage of resources was not a discovery made after defeat. At the Orsha staff conference on 13 November, German officers discussed losses, vehicle availability, railway capacity, and the prospect of continued war in 1942. The figures preserved in the U.S. Army's documentary history are estimates reported within the German command: casualties of approximately 686,000 by 1 November, panzer divisions at roughly thirty-five percent of their original tank strength, and a motor fleet in which only about a third of vehicles were fully serviceable. Such aggregate figures cannot describe every battalion, but they show that the senior leadership knew the army had been profoundly diminished.

The city’s fall appeared to open the lower Don and the routes toward the Caucasus. The Soviet counteroffensive, begun four days earlier, threatened the communications needed to hold that prize. For inhabitants left in Rostov, the change was more immediate: the city had passed under an occupying force whose soldiers would rob, persecute and kill during the brief period of German control.

properties.note: Read The northern war beyond Moscow. Leeb feared that a reduced threat to Moscow would free further Soviet forces for the northern battle. His own advance toward Lake Ladoga had already been stopped near Volkhov on 1 December. German air reconnaissance reported twenty-nine trains moving west along the Vologda–Tikhvin line the next day, a reported movement that heightened concern about reinforcement rather than proving the contents of every train. The intended link with Finnish forces had still not been achieved. Soviet activity around Tikhvin therefore threatened both a vulnerable salient and the larger German hope of tightening the isolation of Leningrad from the east.

properties.note: Read The end of an expectation; Moscow: a counteroffensive in stages; The northern war beyond Moscow; The south after Rostov; Why resources no longer matched objectives; Judgement, weather, and human responsibility; A war that would continue. On the morning of 5 December 1941, Heinz Guderian still hoped to complete the encirclement of Tula. By evening, the commander of Second Panzer Army was proposing to pull his exposed forces back toward the Don and Shat rivers. The change did not represent a sudden discovery that winter existed. It followed repeated failures to eliminate Tula, Soviet pressure against the army's extended positions, and the declining ability of its troops and vehicles to continue offensive operations. One of the commanders most closely associated with German armoured warfare was now trying to preserve the force that had been sent around Moscow's southern flank.

properties.note: Read The end of an expectation; Moscow: a counteroffensive in stages. Farther north, Soviet troops of Ivan Konev's Kalinin Front were beginning counteroffensive operations. The broader attacks associated with the Moscow counteroffensive would develop from 6 December, with different armies entering the fighting at different times. There was no single instant when an entire front turned around. German attacks had continued while Soviet counterattacks were already taking place, and preparations for wider operations had overlapped with the immediate effort to contain dangerous penetrations. The transition was a process experienced unevenly by armies separated by hundreds of kilometres.

properties.note: Read Why resources no longer matched objectives. Guderian's position showed how attack and withdrawal competed for the same diminishing resources. His advanced troops needed fuel to move out of the bulge around Tula, just as they had needed it to close the encirclement. Soviet attacks northeast of Venev threatened the flank and rear of formations already suffering from mechanical failures and restricted movement. Pulling back could shorten their exposure, but the retreat had to begin while they could still move their equipment and maintain contact. By the evening of 5 December, preserving the army had become more urgent than completing the operation that had carried it into those positions.
